name: deheader
desc: Analyze C/C++ files for unnecessary headers
why: Eric Raymond's tool to find unnecessary C headers, a quirky static analysis with a clever trial-and-compile approach.

brief.what_it_is: deheader is a command-line tool, written by Eric S. Raymond, that analyzes C and C++ source files and reports which #include lines can be removed while the code still compiles. It takes one or more source files or a directory (it recurses, skipping dot-directories), and prints a report of removable headers, duplicate includes, and standard headers that portability may require but that are missing. With -r it also rewrites the sources to delete the unneeded includes. It exits 1 when removable includes are found, 2 when a file could not be compiled and analyzed, and 0 otherwise.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it helps find unneeded includes, which can substantially improve compilation time on large C++ projects, and that it sometimes exposes dependencies and cohesions developers did not know about.
brief.how_it_works: For each foo.c, foo.cc or foo.cpp, the test is whether "rm foo.o; make foo.o" returns a zero status, with the build command overridable via -m. Under CMake (when a CMakeLists.txt is detected) it runs "make clean" instead, since foo.o is a phony target there. Inclusions inside #if/#ifdef/#else/#endif blocks are left alone, except headers guarded only by S_SPLINT_S, and each test compile works on a temporary backup of the source that is restored afterward.

brief.install_notes: Packaged for Homebrew under the names deheader and deheader-git, and also distributed as deheader-1.13.tar.gz. The docs do not give a runtime or dependency list. The -i and -x options take Python regular expressions, so a Python runtime is probably needed, but the docs do not say so explicitly. You must have a working build of your own project (make by default, or a custom command via -m) before it can run. No account or configuration is needed.
brief.standout: The tool does not parse C; it brute-forces the answer by deleting each include and asking the real compiler whether the build still succeeds. It works with any build system the user can describe with a command string.
brief.status: Maintained. Homepage and manual are dated 08 Aug 2026 with version 1.13. The Recent Changes list includes several fixes from the last cycle (exit statuses, recoverable source rewriting, option parsing, CMake detection). The manual was last updated 2026-08-08. Repository at gitlab.com/esr/deheader (not fetched).
brief.caveats: With -r it rewrites source files, so the docs insist on version control. Builds of your own project leave many binaries behind, and the docs recommend running make clean afterward. It can produce false positives: headers that only declare prototypes look unneeded unless warnings are fatal. Removing headers can break portability on older Unix systems, especially sockets-related headers, though an internal rule table guards some of them. The docs warn that sufficiently perverse C++ (overloads, template specializations spread across files) can change behavior silently. The docs say it may occasionally remove a header a build needs. The author's Patreon and SubscribeStar links are present, but the license name was not read (COPYING exists). The tool is built around make and CMake, so other build systems need a manual -m string.
